title: Passional Christi und Antichristi — Christ washing the disciples' feet contrasted with the Pope having his feet kissed
creator: Lucas Cranach the Elder (workshop woodcuts); commentary by Philipp Melanchthon and Johann Schwertfeger; published in Wittenberg
repository: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access, CC0)
citation: Lucas Cranach the Elder (workshop), Passional Christi und Antichristi, Wittenberg, 1521. British Museum; public domain.
alt_text: Paired anti-papal woodcuts: on the left, a humble Christ kneels to wash a disciple's foot; on the right, the enthroned Pope in tiara extends his foot to be kissed by kneeling courtiers, mocking clerical worldliness.

title: Der Papstesel (The Pope-Ass of Rome), from 'Deutung der zwei greulichen Figuren'
creator: Lucas Cranach the Elder (workshop woodcut); pamphlet text by Philipp Melanchthon and Martin Luther
repository: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access, CC0)
citation: Lucas Cranach the Elder (workshop), Der Papstesel (Pope-Ass of Rome), in Deutung der zwei greulichen Figuren, Wittenberg, 1523. British Museum; public domain.
alt_text: A grotesque satirical monster with a donkey's head, a woman's scaled body, one clawed hand and one hoofed foot, an ox-leg, and a dragon-headed tail, standing before the Tiber and Castel Sant'Angelo in Rome — Protestant propaganda depicting the papacy as an unnatural beast.

title: King Henry VIII Enthroned Treading upon Pope Clement VII
creator: Woodcut from John Foxe, Acts and Monuments ('Book of Martyrs')
year: 1563 (first edition; woodcut reused in later 16th–17th-c. editions)
repository: HathiTrust — digitized public-domain pre-1929 editions of Foxe's Acts and Monuments
citation: Woodcut, 'Henry VIII treading on Pope Clement VII,' in John Foxe, Acts and Monuments, London, 1563. Public domain; digitized editions at HathiTrust.
alt_text: Protestant propaganda woodcut: King Henry VIII sits enthroned in majesty, sword and orb in hand, with his feet planted on the prostrate body of Pope Clement VII, while bishops look on — visualizing England's break from Rome and royal supremacy over the Church.

title: Sieben Köpffe Martini Luthers (The Seven-Headed Luther)
creator: Hans Brosamer (woodcut) for the Catholic polemicist Johannes Cochlaeus
repository: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access, CC0)
citation: Hans Brosamer (for Johannes Cochlaeus), Sieben Köpffe Martini Luthers (Seven-Headed Luther), 1529. British Museum; public domain.
alt_text: Catholic counter-satire: Martin Luther drawn with seven heads sprouting from a single monk's body — each labeled as a contradictory role (Doctor, Martin, Luther, Ecclesiast, Fanatic, Church Visitor, and Barabbas) — attacking Luther as self-contradictory and heretical.
